questions.question: A refutation prover holds the CNF clauses (¬a∨b) and (¬b∨c). To derive the single clause (¬a∨c) it cancels the complementary literals b and ¬b across two clauses. Which inference rule performs this step?
questions.explanation: Resolution combines two clauses containing complementary literals: from (¬a∨b) and (¬b∨c) it derives the resolvent (¬a∨c). It is a complete inference rule for CNF.

questions.question: A derivation from premise set Γ plus the temporary assumption A ends with B. To close the derivation by writing Γ ⊢ A→B without redoing the steps, which metatheorem is invoked?
questions.explanation: The deduction theorem states that Γ, A ⊢ B implies Γ ⊢ A→B, so deriving B under assumption A licenses discharging A into an implication.

questions.question: To establish that premises Γ yield conclusion φ, a logician inspects every interpretation and finds no model that makes all of Γ true while φ is false. Which notion of consequence — defined by truth preservation in all models — has she verified?
questions.explanation: Semantic consequence (Γ ⊨ φ) is defined model-theoretically: every model of the premises must satisfy the conclusion.

questions.question: Instead of examining models, a proof theorist produces a finite sequence of formulas ending in φ, each step licensed by an inference rule applied to Γ. Which notion of consequence does this derivation establish?
questions.explanation: Syntactic consequence (Γ ⊢ φ) means φ is derivable from Γ using the system's inference rules, with no appeal to models.

questions.question: A proof calculus is advertised as 'complete': for every formula φ that is true in all models of Γ, a derivation of φ from Γ is guaranteed to exist. Which metatheoretic property does the calculus enjoy?
questions.explanation: Completeness says semantic consequence implies syntactic consequence: every semantically valid entailment is provable.

questions.question: A proof system is tested for safety: for every formula φ, the system can prove at most one of φ and ¬φ, and it can never derive p∧¬p. Which property does the system have?
questions.explanation: Consistency means no contradiction is derivable: for no φ does the system prove both φ and ¬φ.

questions.question: A derivation opens with the assumption p, derives q after several steps, then discharges the assumption to record p→q — using only introduction and elimination rules and no axioms. Which Gentzen-style proof system is being used?
questions.explanation: Natural deduction derives conclusions via introduction and elimination rules for each connective, discharging assumptions with →-introduction.

questions.question: Every line of a proof has the shape Γ ⊢ Δ, asserting that the conjunction of the left formulas implies the disjunction of the right formulas. Which Gentzen-style calculus manipulates these sequents?
questions.explanation: Sequent calculus (e.g., Gentzen's LK) reasons about sequents Γ ⊢ Δ via left and right introduction rules for each connective.

questions.question: A sequent proof derives Γ ⊢ A and separately Γ, A ⊢ C, then plugs them together. Gentzen proved any proof built this way can be rewritten to prove Γ ⊢ C directly. Which theorem guarantees this elimination step?
questions.explanation: Cut elimination (Gentzen's Hauptsatz) shows any proof using the cut rule can be transformed into a cut-free proof of the same sequent.

questions.question: A type checker treats the proposition A→B as a function type and a proof of it as a program mapping proofs of A to proofs of B. Which correspondence between logic and computation does this implement?
questions.explanation: The Curry-Howard correspondence identifies propositions with types and proofs with programs inhabiting them.

questions.question: Midway through a sequent proof, the lemma A is already established. To prove Γ ⊢ C, the prover opens two branches: Γ ⊢ A and Γ, A ⊢ C. Which rule permits citing the previously derived lemma this way?
questions.explanation: The cut rule derives Γ ⊢ C from Γ ⊢ A and Γ, A ⊢ C — formally it is what lets a proof reuse an established lemma.

questions.question: A theorem prover is trusted because a metatheorem guarantees that everything derivable from Γ is true in every model of Γ. Which property — provability implies validity — is this?
questions.explanation: Soundness says Γ ⊢ φ implies Γ ⊨ φ: no invalid conclusion is ever provable.

questions.question: After checking that every model making p→q and q→r true also makes p→r true, a logician writes 'p→q, q→r ___ p→r'. Which symbol fills the blank to record semantic consequence?
questions.explanation: The double turnstile ⊨ records semantic entailment: the conclusion holds in every model of the premises.

questions.question: From the single premise p∧¬p a derivation produces the line 'the moon is made of cheese'. Which principle licenses deriving an arbitrary statement once a contradiction is on the board?
questions.explanation: Ex falso quodlibet (the principle of explosion) says a contradiction entails anything: ⊥ ⊢ φ for arbitrary φ.

questions.question: To refute the argument p→q, ¬p ⊢ ¬q, a student exhibits the assignment p=False, q=True, on which both premises are true and the conclusion false. What is such a structure called?
questions.explanation: A countermodel is an interpretation making all premises true and the conclusion false — exactly what demonstrates invalidity.

questions.question: Premises: (1) If the server is patched, the exploit fails. (2) If the exploit fails, the data stays safe. (3) The data did not stay safe. Chaining (1) and (2) and applying modus tollens with (3), what follows about the server?
questions.explanation: p→q and q→r yield p→r by hypothetical syllogism; with ¬r, modus tollens gives ¬p.

questions.question: A resolution refutation uses the clauses (¬p∨q), (p), and (¬q∨r). Resolving the first two clauses produces q; resolving that result with the third clause yields which single literal?
questions.explanation: (¬p∨q) resolves with (p) on p to give (q); (q) resolves with (¬q∨r) on q to give (r).

questions.question: In a 16-row truth table over p, q, r, s, how many rows are counterexamples to the argument p→q, r→s, p∨r ⊢ q∨s?
questions.explanation: This is constructive dilemma, a valid form: whichever of p or r holds forces q or s, so no row makes all premises true with a false conclusion.

questions.question: A proof system derives p∧¬p from an empty premise set. Which metatheoretic property — that every provable formula is semantically valid — must fail?
questions.explanation: p∧¬p is unsatisfiable, so ⊢ p∧¬p holds while ⊭ p∧¬p — violating soundness (and consistency).

questions.question: Premises p→q and ¬p; conclusion ¬q. Under the assignment p=False, q=True both premises are true while the conclusion is false. What does this assignment demonstrate about the argument?
questions.explanation: p→q = F→T = T and ¬p = T, yet ¬q = F: a true-premises/false-conclusion row — the denying-the-antecedent form is invalid.
